q-123355.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14220559/assets/8fbf4c3074641b18d12dc7372378550f4c37e0b9b81843c2e57629c891a59263.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,$ for $\frac{\pi }{3}\le \theta \le \pi ,$ shown above?
q-123355.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }\sqrt{(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }\sqrt{1-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }\sqrt{1-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }\sqrt{5-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cds, where C is the path along the polar curve r=1−2cos⁡θ for π3≤θ≤π, shown above?

a
∫π/3π5+4cos2⁡θdθ
b
∫π/3π1−2cos2⁡θdθ
c
∫π/3π1−2cos⁡θdθ
d
∫π/3π4−5cos2⁡θdθ
e
∫π/3π5−4cos⁡θdθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over C is equal to the arc length L of C, i.e., ∫Cds=L.

In polar coordinates, the arc length element ds is given by

ds=r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

So, for a polar curve defined as r=r(θ) for θ1≤θ≤θ2, we have

L=∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=1−2cos⁡θ, we have drdθ=2sin⁡θ.

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫π/3π(1−2cos⁡θ)2+(2sin⁡θ)2dθ=∫π/3π1−4cos⁡θ+4cos2⁡θ+4sin2⁡θdθ=∫π/3π1−4cos⁡θ+4dθ=∫π/3π5−4cos⁡θdθ.

q-123379.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14220559/assets/19725cfd8068973c899fcb4f54abcebbbfcd24bd68aec510b9d41cee2c2cd02a.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=2-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,$ for $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \pi ,$ shown above?
q-123379.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=2-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi }\sqrt{(2-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi }\sqrt{4-16\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +16{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +16{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi }\sqrt{4-16\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +16}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi }\sqrt{20-16\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi }\sqrt{5-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}

q-123379.html:
Question 2
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cds, where C is the path along the polar curve r=2−4cos⁡θ for π4≤θ≤π, shown above?

a
 2∫π/4π5−2cos⁡2θdθ
b
∫π/4π8−5cos⁡θdθ
c
 4∫π/4π5(1−cos⁡θ)dθ
d
∫π/4π5−4sin⁡θdθ
e
 2∫π/4π5−4cos⁡θdθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over C is equal to the arc length L of C, i.e., ∫Cds=L.

In polar coordinates, the arc length element ds is given by

ds=r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

So, for a polar curve defined as r=r(θ) for θ1≤θ≤θ2, we have

L=∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=2−4cos⁡θ, we have drdθ=4sin⁡θ.

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫π/4π(2−4cos⁡θ)2+(4sin⁡θ)2dθ=∫π/4π4−16cos⁡θ+16cos2⁡θ+16sin2⁡θdθ=∫π/4π4−16cos⁡θ+16dθ=∫π/4π20−16cos⁡θdθ=2∫π/4π5−4cos⁡θdθ.

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=1-5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,$ for $\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{7\pi }{6},$ shown above?
q-123410.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=1-5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{(1-5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{1-10\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +25{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +25{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{1-10\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +25}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{26-10\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cds, where C is the path along the polar curve r=1−5cos⁡θ for π6≤θ≤7π6, shown above?

a
∫π/67π/610−26cos⁡θdθ
b
∫π/67π/68−18cos⁡θdθ
c
∫π/67π/626−10cos⁡θdθ
d
∫π/67π/618−8cos⁡θdθ
e
∫π/67π/616+10cos⁡θdθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over C is equal to the arc length L of C, i.e., ∫Cds=L.

In polar coordinates, the arc length element ds is given by

ds=r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

So, for a polar curve defined as r=r(θ) for θ1≤θ≤θ2, we have

L=∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=1−5cos⁡θ, we have drdθ=5sin⁡θ.

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫π/67π/6(1−5cos⁡θ)2+(5sin⁡θ)2dθ=∫π/67π/61−10cos⁡θ+25cos2⁡θ+25sin2⁡θdθ=∫π/67π/61−10cos⁡θ+25dθ=∫π/67π/626−10cos⁡θdθ.

q-123439.name: Question 4
q-123439.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r={sec}^{3}⁡\theta \,$ for $-\pi /2\le \theta \le \pi /2$ ?
q-123439.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={sec}^{3}⁡\theta \,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=3{sec}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{({sec}^{3}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(3{sec}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{-\pi /2}\sqrt{{sec}^{6}⁡\theta +9{sec}^{6}⁡\theta {tan}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{sec}^{6}⁡\theta (1+9{tan}^{2}⁡\theta })\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{sec}^{3}⁡\theta \sqrt{1+9{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-123439.html:
Question 4
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cds, where C is the path along the polar curve r=sec3⁡θ for −π/2≤θ≤π/2 ?

a
∫0πsec2⁡θtan2⁡θdθ
b
∫−π/2π/2sec3⁡θ1+9tan2⁡θdθ
c
∫0πsec3⁡θ1+tan2⁡θdθ
d
∫−π/2π/2sec3⁡θ9+tan2⁡θdθ
e
2∫0πsec3⁡θ1+sec2⁡θdθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over C is equal to the arc length L of C, i.e., ∫Cds=L.

In polar coordinates, the arc length element ds is given by

ds=r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

So, for a polar curve defined as r=r(θ) for θ1≤θ≤θ2, we have

L=∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=sec3⁡θ we have
drdθ=3sec3⁡θtan⁡θ.

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫−π/2π/2(sec3⁡θ)2+(3sec3⁡θtan⁡θ)2dθ=∫−π/2−π/2sec6⁡θ+9sec6⁡θtan2⁡θdθ=∫−π/2π/2sec6⁡θ(1+9tan2⁡θ)dθ=∫−π/2π/2sec3⁡θ1+9tan2⁡θdθ.

q-123558.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14220559/assets/c27ab9b0062fabfe1fdbfd43631bf1f143c0fa4ec80587519e9ce6c4e84e7b2b.png)

Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},$ shown above.
q-123558.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}(\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}-\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})}) \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\cdot (\sqrt{2}-0) \\  & =4\end{aligned}

Calculate ∫Cds, where C is the path along the polar curve r=1−sin⁡θ for −π2≤θ≤π2, shown above.

EXPLANATION

The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over C is equal to the arc length L of C, i.e., ∫Cds=L.

In polar coordinates, the arc length element ds is given by

ds=r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

So, for a polar curve defined as r=r(θ) for θ1≤θ≤θ2, we have

L=∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=1−sin⁡θ, we have drdθ=−cos⁡θ.

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows: ∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫−π/2π/2(1−sin⁡θ)2+(−cos⁡θ)2dθ=∫−π/2π/21−2sin⁡θ+sin2⁡θ+cos2⁡θdθ=2∫−π/2π/21−sin⁡θdθ=221+sin⁡θ|−π/2π/2=22(1+sin⁡(π2)−1+sin⁡(−π2))=22⋅(2−0)=4
